passage:
Monday: Vidya laughed when Reena mispronounced a word in reading circle. Before Reena even knew it, her eraser flew across the room and hit Vidya's shoulder. By lunch Reena felt awful and couldn't eat her lemon rice.
Tuesday: Reena's class teacher, Mrs Dutta, gave her a secret word. 'When the hot feeling comes, say "pineapple" in your head and count three fingers on your desk. Then choose.'
Friday: In maths, Vidya snorted at Reena's wrong answer. Reena's hand closed around her pencil. Pineapple. One, two, three fingers. She put the pencil down and said, 'That wasn't nice, Vidya.' Vidya went red and muttered sorry. Reena grinned all through recess.

qa.q: What secret word did Mrs Dutta give Reena?
qa.a: Pineapple, said in her head while counting three fingers on the desk.

qa.q: How did Reena feel after throwing the eraser, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She felt awful and sorry; she couldn't eat her lemon rice at lunch.

qa.q: What turning point on Friday showed the cue word working?
qa.a: When Vidya snorted, Reena thought pineapple, counted three fingers and chose words instead of throwing, telling Vidya it wasn't nice.

qa.q: How might Vidya see Reena after Friday?
qa.a: Vidya may feel embarrassed and start to see that teasing Reena hurts, since Reena named it calmly instead of lashing out.

grounding: Shows a child who throws something in anger and feels sorry later, and a cue word and pause that widen the gap between urge and action.

passage:
Lavanya, come, sit by your Salma aunty. You think you're the only one whose mouth runs ahead? When I was ten, at our school in Bhopal, I shouted answers before the teacher finished. I pushed to the front of the water queue. Once I tore my friend's drawing because she laughed at mine, and then cried all night, because I loved that girl.
My Abba didn't beat me or call me bad. He taught me a trick. Before I did anything with a hot face, I had to press my thumb to each finger, one by one. Four little taps.
By the time I reached my little finger, the shout had usually gone quieter. Not always! But more and more.
I still do it, you know. In queues at the bank.

qa.q: What trick did Abba teach Salma?
qa.a: To press the thumb to each finger, one by one, four little taps, before doing anything with a hot face.

qa.q: How did Salma feel after tearing the friend's drawing, and why?
qa.a: She felt deep regret and cried all night, because she loved that friend.

qa.q: Which choice by Abba helped Salma more than punishment would have?
qa.a: He didn't beat her or call her bad; he gave her a simple pause, the finger taps, that widened the gap between the hot feeling and acting.

qa.q: How might Lavanya feel hearing that Salma aunty once had the same trouble?
qa.a: Lavanya might feel less alone and less ashamed, and more willing to try the four taps.

grounding: Shows, through an elder's memory, a child who blurted, pushed and tore things in anger and felt sorry, and a pause habit that widened the gap before acting.

passage:
Thursday. Did it again. In the lunch queue Mohit said our team lost because of me, and before I even knew it, I threw my steel tumbler at the wall. It clanged so loud everyone went silent. Sir made me pick it up. Mohit looked scared, which made me feel horrible. I didn't mean to scare him. It's like my hand moves before my head. Sir said we'd try a secret word: when he says "mango", I put my hands in my pockets and count to five. I think it's silly. But after lunch I said sorry to Mohit, and tomorrow I'll try the mango thing.
Harish

qa.q: What did Harish throw at the wall?
qa.a: The steel tumbler.

qa.q: How did Harish feel after seeing Mohit look scared?
qa.a: Harish felt horrible and sorry, not having meant to scare Mohit.

qa.q: How could the secret word help Harish?
qa.a: Hearing "mango" and counting to five with hands in pockets widens the gap between the angry urge and the action.

qa.q: How might Mohit have felt when the tumbler clanged?
qa.a: Mohit was scared and shocked, even though he had started the argument.

grounding: Shows a child who throws something in anger before thinking, then feels sorry and tries a cue word to pause.

passage: In the one-room school at Sonpur, Vijay's hand shot up before Jahnavi-didi finished every question, and when it didn't, his mouth did. "Seventeen!" "The Ganga!" Today at the hand pump he shoved past three smaller children to fill his bottle first, and one of them fell in the mud. Vijay's face burned; he helped her up, mumbling sorry. After class Jahnavi-didi didn't scold. She drew a small clock on his wrist in pen. "When you want to shout or push, touch the clock and breathe once. Just once." Next morning a question came. Vijay's hand twitched. He touched the clock. He breathed. Then he raised his hand, and waited.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi-didi draw on Vijay's wrist?
qa.a: A small clock.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel after the child fell in the mud?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and sorry, his face burning.

qa.q: Why might the pen clock work?
qa.a: It gives Vijay a quick cue to pause and breathe, widening the gap between urge and action.

qa.q: What is it like for the smaller children when Vijay shoves past?
qa.a: They are pushed aside and one falls in the mud, which is upsetting and unfair.

grounding: Illustrates a child who blurts and pushes before thinking, then uses a simple cue to pause.

passage: At football practice in Hamburg, Felix scored on Oskar for the third time, and Oskar kicked the ball straight at his back. It hit hard. Felix spun round, shocked. The anger drained out of Oskar at once, and a sick feeling came instead. "Sorry, I didn't... it just happened." Coach Anna blew the whistle and knelt beside him. "I believe you didn't plan it. Your feet were faster than your thinking. Let's make a pause button. When you feel that hot rush, say 'stop' in your head and take one big step back." They practised three times, Oskar feeling silly. In the next game Felix scored again. Oskar's leg lifted. He whispered "stop", stepped back, and went to shake Felix's hand.

qa.q: How many times had Felix scored on Oskar when Oskar kicked the ball?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: How did Oskar feel right after the ball hit Felix?
qa.a: The anger drained away and he felt sick and sorry.

qa.q: What pause did Coach Anna teach, and why does it help?
qa.a: Saying "stop" in his head and stepping back, which gives Oskar time between the hot rush and acting.

qa.q: How might Felix feel when Oskar shakes his hand?
qa.a: Felix may feel relieved and respected after being hit earlier.

grounding: Shows a child who acts in anger before thinking, feels sorry and learns a pause cue that widens the gap.

passage:
In the Class 4 classroom, Farida's hand shot up before Ma'am finished the question, and she shouted the answer. At lunch she pushed ahead of Pankaj in the water queue. When he said, "Hey!", she threw her eraser at him.
A second later her face fell. "Sorry! I didn't mean to."
After lunch, the class teacher, Ms Joseph, took her aside, not angry. "Your body moves faster than your thinking. Let's make a gap. When you feel the rush, squeeze your pencil and say 'pause' inside your head. Just one breath."
Farida tried it the next day. The question came, her hand twitched, and she squeezed her pencil. She waited until Ma'am said "Anyone?"
In the queue, she felt the push rising again. Pencil squeeze. Pause. She stayed behind Pankaj, and he turned round and smiled.

qa.q: What did Farida throw at Pankaj?
qa.a: Her eraser.

qa.q: How did Farida feel right after throwing the eraser?
qa.a: She felt sorry and ashamed, her face falling as she said she didn't mean to.

qa.q: What cue did Ms Joseph teach, and why did it help?
qa.a: Squeezing her pencil and saying "pause" inside her head, which widened the gap between the urge and the action.

qa.q: How might Pankaj see Farida by the end?
qa.a: Pankaj, who was pushed and hit with an eraser, now sees her waiting her turn, which is why he turns and smiles.

grounding: Shows an impulsive child who blurts, pushes and throws in anger then feels sorry, and a cue word and pause that widen the gap.
